one_liner: Zig word-hash codec (Density-style) that encodes faster than lz4 --fast=20 and zstd --fast=5, at a lower ratio.
what_it_does: Firetrail is a Zig CLI and library with three codecs that replace each aligned 8-byte word by a 2-byte hash when the word is already in a 64K-entry (512 KB) table. White never updates the table and needs a trained dictionary (--import), Orange overwrites the slot on every miss, and Red only replaces slots whose frequency counter has decayed to zero. The CLI streams 8 MiB blocks with a raw-size and compressed-size header per block; the library API is a pair of Zig generic structs (compressBlockToBuffer / decompressBlockToBuffer) with no C ABI, so it is not a drop-in for lz4 or zstd.
how_it_is_fast: There is no match search or entropy coding: each 64-bit word costs one Fibonacci multiplicative hash, one table load and one compare, and every 8 words share a 1-byte flag header, so the loop is branch-light, unrolled at compile time (inline for) and built with runtime safety off. The README describes the design as inspired by Density. Because only whole words at 8-byte-aligned positions can match, the best possible ratio is about 3.76x (8 bytes become 2 bytes plus 1/8 of a header byte).
when_to_use: Experiments with very fast single-thread encoding of large, repetitive, word-aligned data such as logs (HDFS.log: Orange 2.42 GB/s encode at 2.53x versus lz4 --fast=20 at 1.25 GB/s and 4.53x).
A deployed static dictionary (White) for streams that share a vocabulary, where the dictionary is trained once with Red and shipped to both ends.
Pipelines that are encode-bound and can accept a ratio of 1.2-1.5x on mixed data, in a Zig code base.
Reading the code as a compact reference for Density-style word hashing (about 180 lines per codec).
when_not_to_use: Any production or redistributed use: the repository has no LICENSE file, so the code cannot legally be copied.

Incompressible or already-compressed input with the CLI: an 8 MiB block of random data encodes to 8,519,680 bytes, but the decoder reads each compressed block into an 8,388,608-byte buffer (input_data_bound = block_size in main.zig), so such files cannot be decoded and, in ReleaseFast builds, the read overruns the heap buffer.

Untrusted input: decompressBlockToBuffer runs with @setRuntimeSafety(false) and never checks the compressed length, and the CLI trusts the per-block sizes in the stream; there is no checksum or format magic.
Decode-bound workloads: lz4 decodes faster on all four corpora (silesia 2.53 versus 1.89 GB/s for White).
When ratio matters: lz4 and zstd compress smaller on silesia and HDFS.log, and zstd --fast=5 beats it everywhere on ratio.

integration.dependencies: none at run time; zBench (Zig) for the in-memory benchmark target
integration.platforms: any Zig target in principle (portable code, explicit little-endian I/O, no SIMD intrinsics); benchmarks only on x86-64 Linux (Ryzen 7 7800X3D)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; each encoder/decoder owns a mutable 512 KB table, so use one instance per thread

gotchas: Encoder and decoder must start from identical tables: a White or Orange stream encoded with --import dict.bin decodes to wrong bytes without that same file, and nothing in the stream records which dictionary or codec was used.
White without an imported dictionary compresses almost nothing, because its table starts zeroed and is never updated.
No round-trip check anywhere: the algorithm files have no tests, and scripts/bench.fish times decode with poop but never compares the decoded file with the original.
The published White figures use a dictionary trained on the very file being compressed and leave its 512 KB out of the size, so Orange is the fair cold comparison.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against LZ4, Density and ZXC it only wins on single-thread encode speed for word-aligned repetitive data; pick LZ4 (or memlz for encode-only speed) for anything that needs decode speed, a stable format, a C API or a licence, and Density if you want this style of word-hash codec with a licence and a library API.
verified_claims_summary: The author's end-to-end CLI timings (poop, single thread, warm page cache, Ryzen 7 7800X3D, CachyOS, Zig release-fast build versus distro lz4 1.10.0 --fast=20 and zstd 1.5.7 --fast=5, all -T1) put silesia.tar encode at 1.67 GB/s for White and 1.54 GB/s for Orange versus 0.98 GB/s for lz4 and 0.69 GB/s for zstd, with Orange's ratio 1.54x against lz4's 1.56x; geomean over four corpora is 1.6x lz4 and 2.5x zstd for White. Decoded output was not verified in the harness, and the independent lzbench row covers the predecessor skim 0.1.0, not this codec.
status_note: Active hobby project (63 commits, last 2026-08-04, version 0.0.0, 1 star) with no licence, so treat it as a reference to read rather than code to vendor.
